extracted.intended_audience: Researchers applying for ERC grants; ERC evaluation panel members and ERC Executive Agency staff
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rules for evaluating ERC research grant proposals (2024 changes), describing which characteristics of projects and applicants are considered, how they are weighed and scored, and how CV/track-record information should be presented and used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sole criterion: scientific excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The ERC's sole legal evaluation criterion is scientific excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels must judge applications on scientific excellence only and should not include economic or societal impact as explicit evaluation criteria (to avoid disfavouring fundamental, curiosity-driven research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Project excellence: ground‑breaking nature, ambition and feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals are primarily evaluated on the ground‑breaking nature, ambition and feasibility of the research project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels should assess creativity, originality and potential for significant advances in knowledge, and the scientific approach, emphasising the proposed research content over other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred terminology: ambitious / creative / original (avoid 'high‑risk, high‑gain')
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'high‑risk, high‑gain' is considered confusing/problematic for evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should prefer descriptors like 'ambitious', 'creative' and 'original' when assessing the kinds of proposals ERC should fund; do not require unpredictability of outcome as a defining feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel methodology development (not necessary nor sufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Development of novel methodologies can be positive but is neither necessary nor sufficient for an excellent proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects should be assessed on their core questions and approaches; evaluators are not specifically asked about development of new methodologies in the project evaluation guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant: intellectual capacity, creativity and relevant expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels evaluate the applicant's intellectual capacity and creativity, focusing on whether the applicant has the scientific expertise and capacity to successfully execute the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of the PI should determine ability to carry out ambitious research, primarily via their track record (research outputs and peer recognition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined CV/track record template (four pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: The CV and track record are combined into a single template limited to four pages (fixed font and spacing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants decide how to allocate space across the template's three sections (personal details; research achievements and peer recognition; additional information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Research achievements: up to ten outputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may list up to ten research outputs with an emphasis on more recent achievements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The type of output is deliberately left open (publications, preprints, books/essays, datasets, code, expeditions, patents, prototypes, etc.). For each entry applicants are encouraged to provide a brief narrative explaining how it advanced the field and demonstrates capacity to carry out the proposed project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer recognition (context for track record)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer recognition can be included (prizes, awards, academy memberships, honorary degrees, leadership positions, etc.) to provide context to the track record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The new template no longer asks for specific peer recognition elements but leaves it to applicants to list and narratively explain the significance and context of items; panels are given explicit guidance to take field and career-stage differences into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional information: career breaks, diverse paths, life events, community contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: A section where applicants can provide context such as career breaks, diverse research career paths, major life events, and noteworthy contributions to the research community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This information provides context for the evaluation of achievements and peer recognition, but is not the primary basis for assessing scientific excellence of the proposed project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative CV elements (subjectivity and controls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative elements are allowed to complement quantitative information but are subjective and less standardised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reduce problems (misrepresentation, cultural differences in self-promotion, variable writing skills), the section is length-limited, applicants are asked to explain achievements in neutral terms, and panels are warned to be wary of boastful applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use quantity proxies (e.g., number of publications) as primary measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations should focus on quality rather than quantity of outputs; inappropriate surrogate metrics should not be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel members are instructed to avoid using Journal Impact Factors and other surrogate measures; quantitative metrics must be used responsibly and focus should be on scientific content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit outputs shown to alleviate reading burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Because evaluators cannot read every output, applicants are limited to selecting and explaining a limited number of outputs (ten) with emphasis on recent ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps panels judge significance without requiring exhaustive reading; applicants should choose outputs that best demonstrate capacity for the proposed project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision of students/postdocs: do not ask raw counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers of supervised PhD students or postdocs are not requested as a measure of mentorship quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raw supervision counts are unreliable across disciplines and institutions and can be proxies for environment rather than mentorship; no reliable, fair alternative was found for ERC-wide use, so the element was removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramural funding: not a primary quality metric
rubrics_metrics.description: Amount of extramural funding attracted should not be used to judge the importance or competitiveness of a researcher's work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding levels vary by national context and research type; ERC will consider prior funding only to ensure the proposed project is not already funded and only at the second step of evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of other contributions (teaching, peer review, leadership) as context
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions like teaching, peer review, committee work, academic leadership and outreach are valuable and should be recognised, but are peripheral to assessing the ability to carry out the proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly noteworthy community contributions may be listed to provide context but they do not directly enter the primary evaluation of research achievements and peer recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panels must not consider host institution in assessing applicant excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: The host institution should not be an element that enters the evaluation of the applicant's excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators must avoid institutional prestige biases (Matthew effects); the removal of certain track-record elements (e.g., list of previously funded grants) helps mitigate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of assessment: evaluate project before applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: During individual remote evaluation, panel members first evaluate the research project without considering applicant information, then evaluate the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces the risk that applicant identity or reputation will influence the project score and helps emphasise the project in initial ranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring and weighting: numeric project score; qualitative applicant assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Only the project is scored on a numerical scale and used to rank proposals before panel discussion; the applicant receives an overall qualitative assessment with five options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant assessment categories (outstanding, excellent, very good, good, non-competitive) are not converted to numbers and are not combined with the project score, so the project receives more weight and numerical combination that amplified bias is avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double‑blind review impractical for ERC
rubrics_metrics.description: Double‑blind review was deemed almost impossible because assessing capacity to carry out a project requires knowledge of the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of full anonymity, the process separates project and applicant evaluation order to minimise bias while retaining applicant information for suitability judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prescriptive guidance while providing clear evaluation elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance should help panels and applicants understand expectations without being overly prescriptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels need freedom to exercise expertise, but consistent, non-prescriptive written guidance and briefings are provided to limit sub-optimal heuristics and increase fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Template: personal details section limited to factual career overview
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal details section includes education, training, current and past positions, and brief factual comments about career steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments about non-research work, career breaks or special aspects should be placed in the additional information section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance: provide examples for research achievements and peer recognition only
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance for applicants provides examples for categories of research achievements and peer recognition but not for 'other contributions to the research community'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids implying a limited list of acceptable 'other contributions' and helps applicants understand the main expected evidence formats for track record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative explanations: request neutral, factual descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants are instructed to include short, factual explanations of the significance of selected outputs, their role in producing them, and how they demonstrate capacity to carry out the proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutral phrasing aims to mitigate cultural differences in self-presentation and reduce the advantage of strong rhetorical skills over scientific merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible use of metrics (avoid Journal Impact Factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel members are instructed to refrain from using surrogate measures such as the Journal Impact Factor when evaluating applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative indicators may be used responsibly but should not substitute reading and assessing the scientific content of outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open science practices (can be reported but are not mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open access to publications, data and other research outputs is a dimension that may be reported in track record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open science practices can inform assessment but are not required for demonstrating ability to carry out the proposed research; panels should not disadvantage applicants for different practices across fields or contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation leadership and technological impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of innovation leadership (patents, prototypes, technological impact) can be included in the research achievements portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such outputs are legitimate evidence of research achievement where relevant to the field and should be explained in narratives to demonstrate their significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track record in funding (contextual only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to acquire third‑party funds and wins of competitive funding are an item on the list of potential dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because funding opportunities differ by context, this is not used as a primary quality metric at the first step, and prior funding is considered mainly to check for double funding at a later stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborations and interdisciplinarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Development of multi-, inter-, trans- or cross-disciplinary activities, leadership of collaborative projects, maintaining international collaborations and intersectoral collaborations are recognised dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels should take into account collaborative and interdisciplinary evidence when relevant to the project's success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advancement and enablement of junior researchers
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that a PI nurtures talent (e.g., high research student completion rates, enabling others' excellence) is a listed dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While important, quantitative proxies are problematic; particularly noteworthy contributions in this area may be mentioned in additional information to provide context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching and mentoring activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular teaching activity, workshops, summer schools, and mentoring are recognised contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities can be listed as context but should not replace evidence of the PI's ability to carry out frontier research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research community service and integrity contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing, reviewing, refereeing, committee work, organising events, contributions to research integrity and culture, and appointments to positions of responsibility are dimensions to report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such contributions are valuable for the research ecosystem and may be acknowledged in the application to provide context but are not the primary basis for assessing the proposal's scientific excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader-society engagement (citizen science, outreach, policy advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement with the public, policymaking, industry, or wider society (including science communication, media interactions, exhibitions) is a recognised dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities can be reported as contributions but economic or societal impact should not be used as an explicit evaluation criterion for ERC project excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental perspective: career stage, independence and mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Career stage, leadership potential, research independence, and international/intersectoral mobility are relevant contextual dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels should account for career-stage differences when judging track record and capacity to carry out proposed research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal context and diversity considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconventional career paths, career breaks, part‑time work, personal circumstances, underrepresented group membership, and broader diversity considerations are to be reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These personal context items provide important context for fair assessment; panels are instructed to consider them and avoid disadvantaging applicants for such reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics, integrity and freedom of research
rubrics_metrics.description: General and research-specific ethics and integrity standards must be met; freedom of scientific research and security issues are listed considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must comply with ethics standards; panels should be mindful of integrity and freedom of research in evaluation context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding unintended biases and panel functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel selection, composition and functioning can introduce biases; careful selection of panel members and possible roles for agency scientific officers were discussed to reduce 'scientific community games'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Briefings and consistent guidance aim to improve panel functioning; the Scientific Council will monitor and refine procedures to reduce biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial randomisation as an allocation approach (experimental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial randomisation (lottery) is an innovative approach suggested for allocation within the 'grey zone' where panels disagree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial randomisation can be considered to reduce subjective factors and encourage risk-taking research, but implementation and effects require further study and are not a current evaluation criterion.
